rows.jp: 帰路を歩く。
rows.en: I walk home.

ghs.en: Walking on the road home.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi walks home. The English is a subjectless participial fragment and literalizes the route as a road.

rows.jp: 「うーむ」
rows.en: “Hmm.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Mmmh-hmm."

rows.jp: 結局、何もない一日を過ごしてしまった。
rows.en: In the end, I let another uneventful day slip by.

ghs.en: In the end, one whole day passed with nothing done.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says he ended up spending an uneventful day. The English says the day itself passed and changes absence of events into failure to do anything.

highlights.text: one whole day passed with nothing done

rows.jp: リセットがかかると知っているせいかな。
rows.en: Maybe it’s because I know everything will reset.

ghs.en: Perhaps, knowing that it will all be reset is to blame.

rows.jp: どうも身が入らない。
rows.en: I just can’t put my heart into anything.

ghs.en: Somehow I just wasn't into things.

rows.jp: それに……学校に行っても賑やかさは感じられない。
rows.en: Besides... even at school, nothing feels lively.

ghs.en: Besides... I might have gone to school, but I cannot feel its bustling liveliness.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that even when he goes to school, he cannot feel any liveliness. The English turns his actual attendance into an uncertain past possibility.

highlights.text: I might have gone to school

rows.jp: 世界はガラスキになっている。
rows.en: The world has emptied out.

ghs.en: The world had become almost entirely uninhabited.
ghs.assessment: ガラスキ says the world is largely empty or sparsely populated. 'Almost entirely uninhabited' intensifies that state, and past perfect lacks a later past anchor.

rows.jp: 八人では世界とは言えない。
rows.en: Eight people are not enough to call a world.

ghs.en: With eight people one cannot call it a world.

rows.jp: 永遠の一夏。
rows.en: One eternal summer.

ghs.en: A single eternal Summer...

rows.jp: 俺たちは、時の渦にとらわれた人類の残骸なんだろうか。
rows.en: Are we the remnants of humanity, trapped in a whirlpool of time?

ghs.en: We might just be the wreckage of mankind caught in the swirl of an eddy of time.
ghs.assessment: 時の渦 is simply the vortex or eddy of time. The English redundantly places an eddy inside a separate swirl.

highlights.text: swirl of an eddy of time

rows.jp: それとも……別の意味が。
rows.en: Or is there... some other meaning?

ghs.en: Or perhaps... it means something else.

rows.jp: 坂の途中、立ち止まる。
rows.en: Partway along the slope, I stop.

ghs.en: Midway through a hill, I come to a halt.
ghs.assessment: 坂の途中 means partway up or down a slope. 'Through a hill' suggests passage inside or across the landform.

rows.jp: 道の脇にある雑木林。
rows.en: The roadside copse.

ghs.en: On the side of the road there is a grove of trees.

rows.jp: 思い出す。
rows.en: I remember.

ghs.en: I remember.

rows.jp: 思い出す……。
rows.en: I remember...

ghs.en: I remember...

rows.jp: 新川豊が雑木林を眺めていた。
rows.en: Yutaka Shinkawa was staring into a copse.

ghs.en: Shinkawa Yutaka was gazing lost at a grove of trees.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says only that he was gazing at the grove. 'Lost' invents a mental state and is not grammatically integrated as an adverb.

rows.jp: 俺はそんな新川のもとに近寄り、声をかける。
rows.en: I walked over to Shinkawa and called out to him.

ghs.en: As I was drawing nearer to Shinkawa as he was, I called out to him.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi approaches Shinkawa and speaks to him. The English repeats 'as' and adds a meaningless trailing state clause.

highlights.text: As I was drawing nearer to Shinkawa as he was

rows.jp: 「どうした？」
rows.en: “What is it?”

ghs.en: Taichi: "What is it?"

rows.jp: 新川は汗をかいていた。
rows.en: Shinkawa was sweating.

ghs.en: Shinkawa was sweating.

rows.jp: 見るからに夏の汗ではない。
rows.en: Plainly not from the summer heat.

ghs.en: On closer look, that's not the sweat of the heat of Summer.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says it is clearly not ordinary summer sweat. The English stacks two possessive prepositional phrases and capitalizes the season.

highlights.text: the sweat of the heat of Summer

rows.jp: よろと後ずさる。
rows.en: He stumbled backward.

ghs.en: He staggers back, unsteady.

rows.jp: 車が来た。
rows.en: A vehicle came.

ghs.en: A car came.

rows.jp: 「新川！」
rows.en: “Shinkawa!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "SHINKAWA!"

rows.jp: 新川は轢かれて死んだ。それは俺のトラウマになった。
rows.en: Shinkawa was run over and killed. It left me traumatized.

ghs.en: Shinkawa is struck, tumbles down and dies. That was the origin of my psychological trauma.

rows.jp: ……などということはなく、
rows.en: ...Except nothing like that happened.

ghs.en: ...and all other things of that sort that didn't happen.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese retracts the immediately preceding imagined event: nothing like that happened. The English invents multiple other events and attaches them to an ungoverned coordination.

highlights.text: and all other things of that sort that didn't happen

rows.jp: 「あ、田崎商店のデコ軽トラだ」
rows.en: “Oh, it’s the decorated mini-truck from Tazaki Shop.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Ah, it's the Tasaki Store's decorated company truck."
ghs.assessment: 軽トラ is a kei pickup truck. The English adds that it is a company vehicle rather than merely belonging to or advertising the store.

rows.jp: ド派手なソイツが、時速三十キロでゆっくりと通り過ぎていく。
rows.en: The wildly gaudy thing rolled slowly past at thirty kilometers an hour.

ghs.en: That hideously flashy thing passes us by at the leisurely speed of about thirty kilometers an hour.

rows.jp: 福顔のオヤジが、俺に向かって『いつもありがと～』と手を振った。
rows.en: The genial old man waved at me. ‘Thanks as always!’

ghs.en: That smiling guy waved a 'thank you for everythi～ng' towards me and waved his hand.
ghs.assessment: The driver calls out the thanks while waving. The English makes the words themselves an object he waves, then redundantly says he waves his hand.

highlights.text: waved a 'thank you for everythi～ng' towards me and waved his hand

rows.jp: 俺はお得意様だから。
rows.en: I was one of his best customers.

ghs.en: Because I am quite the profitable customer.
ghs.assessment: お得意様 means a valued regular customer. 'Profitable' introduces the store's economic assessment and need not follow from being a regular.

rows.jp: 振り返した。
rows.en: I waved back.

ghs.en: I returned the gesture.

rows.jp: 「昭和時代のマニアックな飲料水の入荷、いつもありがとー！」
rows.en: “And thanks as always for stocking obscure soft drinks from the Showa era!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Thank you for always stocking up on soft drinks for us Showa era fanatiiics!"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese thanks the shop for stocking obscure Showa-era beverages. The English instead describes the drinkers, including Taichi, as Showa fanatics.

highlights.text: soft drinks for us Showa era fanatiiics

rows.jp: アン○サ。
rows.en: AM○SA.

ghs.en: Am*sa

rows.jp: メ○ーイエロー。
rows.en: Me○ Yello.

ghs.en: Me**o Yello.

rows.jp: ネーポ○。
rows.en: Nepo○.

ghs.en: Neepo*.

rows.jp: 胡椒警部。
rows.en: Inspector Pepper.

ghs.en: Inspector Pepper.

rows.jp: ゲータ○ード。
rows.en: Gator○de.

ghs.en: Gato**de

rows.jp: 伝説のソフトドリンクたち。
rows.en: Legendary soft drinks, one and all.

ghs.en: Legendary soft drink-tachi.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese plural suffix たち simply groups the legendary soft drinks. The English leaves it as an unexplained Japanese suffix on an English singular noun.

rows.jp: 元鉄オタだからビジネスもマニアックなのだろうか。
rows.en: Maybe being a former railfan explains why his business is so specialized.

ghs.en: He's a former railway otaku, so that's likely why he's equally fanatical about his business.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese wonders whether his business is similarly niche because he used to be a train geek. It does not say he is fanatically devoted to commerce.

rows.jp: どうやって入荷しているのかは知らない。
rows.en: I have no idea how he procures them.

ghs.en: How exactly he manages to get them in stock I don't know.

rows.jp: とにかく新川は死ななかった。
rows.en: In any event, Shinkawa did not die.

ghs.en: Anyway, Shinkawa hadn't died.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese concludes the immediately imagined incident by saying Shinkawa did not die. Past perfect incorrectly places that non-event before a later past anchor.

rows.jp: ピンピンしてる。
rows.en: He was fit as a fiddle.

ghs.en: He was happy and lively.
ghs.assessment: ピンピンしている means that he is alive and perfectly healthy or energetic. The English adds emotional happiness.

rows.jp: 「今おまえは生死の境を彷徨った。俺がこうしてがっしと腕をキャッチしなかったら、その灰色の脳細胞はアスファルトの上でグロ画像になっていただろう」
rows.en: “You just wandered the boundary between life and death. If I hadn’t caught you firmly by the arm, those gray cells of yours would have become a gore pic on the asphalt.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "You've wandered into the boundary between life and death right then. If I hadn't gone and caught your arm, those gray brain cells of yours would've become a Guro Scene over the asphalt."
ghs.assessment: グロ画像 means a graphic or gore image. The English leaves guro unexplained and capitalizes the resulting phrase as a named scene.

rows.jp: 新川は震えていた。
rows.en: Shinkawa was trembling.

ghs.en: Shinkawa was shaking.

rows.jp: 「新川？」
rows.en: “Shinkawa?”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Shinkawa?"

rows.jp: 「あ……悪い」
rows.en: “Oh... sorry.”

ghs.en: Shinkawa: "Ah... my bad."

rows.jp: 我に返る。
rows.en: He came back to himself.

ghs.en: He returns to his senses.

rows.jp: 「なんか……雑木林の奥とか見てたら……すげぇ気分悪くなってきて……昔から、そうなんだけどさ……わけ、わかんねぇんだけど……」
rows.en: “I don’t know... I looked deep into the trees and... started feeling really sick... It’s always been like that... I don’t know why...”

ghs.en: Shinkawa: "It's jus'... when I look like deep in the trees... I get this really bad feelin' and stuff... it's been like that since a long time ago... why, I totally dun'no tho..."
ghs.assessment: The rough colloquial source supports informality, but these phrases misuse 'like,' pair 'since' with a duration, and invent a malformed contraction.

highlights.text: look like deep in the trees

rows.jp: 顔を手で覆って、立ちくらみに戸惑うように、しばし。
rows.en: He covered his face with one hand and stood there for a while, as if bewildered by a dizzy spell.

ghs.en: He covers his face with his hand, as if puzzled by his own dizziness, for a time.

rows.jp: 青い空を見あげて、喘ぐように息を吐いた。
rows.en: Then he looked up at the blue sky and let out a gasping breath.

ghs.en: He then looked up at the blue sky, gasping as if pained.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he exhales as though gasping. The English adds pain and makes 'gasping' modify his looking up rather than the breath.

ghs.en: Taichi: "......"

rows.jp: 『俺、足が片方あんま動かなくてさ』
rows.en: ‘One of my legs doesn’t move very well.’

ghs.en: Shinkawa: 『Me, I can't really move one of my legs.』

rows.jp: 外障だと思っていた。
rows.en: I had thought he was classified under physical impairment.

ghs.en: I had thought he was External Damage.
ghs.assessment: 外障 abbreviates an external disability. 'Damage' describes injury to an object, not a person's disability, and the capitalization invents an official category name.

rows.jp: 群青にも少数ながら、外部障害保持者を受け入れる枠はあったから。
rows.en: Gunjo did have a small number of places for students classified under physical impairment.

ghs.en: While in Gunjou they were a minority, there was a minimum quota of Persons Operating with External Impediments.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says Gunjō had a small admissions category for people with external disabilities. The English changes that to a minimum quota, uses a euphemistic invented title, and romanizes the place name nonstandardly.

highlights.text: While in Gunjou they were a minority, there was a minimum quota of Persons Operating with External Impediments.

rows.jp: けど豊は内障……内部障害だったのかも知れない。今にして思えば。
rows.en: But perhaps Yutaka had an internal... an internal impairment. Looking back now.

ghs.en: But could Yutaka have been Internal Damage... Operating with Internal Impediment. Maybe. In retrospect,
ghs.assessment: 内障 and 内部障害 refer to an internal disability. The English first calls the person damage, then invents a capitalized euphemistic bureaucratic label.

rows.jp: 森の中。
rows.en: Inside a forest.

ghs.en: in the middle of the woods,

rows.jp: 木々に囲まれた閉鎖空間。
rows.en: An enclosed space ringed by trees.

ghs.en: in a sealed space surrounded by trees,

rows.jp: 俺も苦手だった。
rows.en: I had trouble with places like that, too.

ghs.en: I would also have felt ill at ease.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese states that Taichi was also uncomfortable in such spaces. The conditional perfect turns that fact into a hypothetical.

rows.jp: 昔、心に傷を穿(うが)つ出来事があった。
rows.en: Long ago, something happened that gouged a wound into my heart.

ghs.en: A long time ago, there had been an event that had drilled a wound upon my heart.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese metaphor says an event once gouged a wound into his heart. The English doubles past perfect and uses the wrong preposition with the literal drilling image.

highlights.text: there had been an event that had drilled a wound upon my heart

rows.jp: 新川の気持ちを、だから俺は少し理解することができた。
rows.en: That was why I could understand a little of what Shinkawa felt.

ghs.en: And I could, therefore, manage to comprehend Shinkawa's feelings a little.
